title: What is TDD (Test-Driven Development) — write the test FIRST (it fails), then write just enough code to make it pass, then refactor — the Red-Green-Refactor cycle — and why does it help (catches bugs early, better design, acts as documentation)?
shortTitle: What is TDD (Test-Driven Development) and the Red-Green-Refactor cycle

s1_definition.profdef: Test-Driven Development is a development practice where you write a failing test before writing the production code. The cycle is Red, write a small test that fails because the behavior does not exist yet; Green, write the minimum code to make that test pass; Refactor, clean up the design while keeping the test green. You repeat this in tight loops. It helps because it catches bugs at the moment of writing, drives simpler and more testable design since code is written to satisfy a test, and leaves a suite of tests that documents exactly what the code is supposed to do.
s1_definition.analogy: When building the National Bank of India interest calculator, instead of writing the calculator and hoping it works, you first write a tiny check that says "for one hundred thousand rupees at four percent for one year, the interest must be four thousand." It fails because there is no calculator yet, that is Red. Then you write just enough calculator code to make that check pass, that is Green. Then you tidy the code without breaking the check, that is Refactor. You keep adding one small check at a time. The result is that every rule is proven as you build it, the design stays simple because you only write what a check demands, and the checks themselves become a living description of how interest is meant to work.
s1_definition.oneliner: TDD means write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor, repeating this Red-Green-Refactor loop, which catches bugs early, drives simpler testable design, and leaves tests that document the intended behavior.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Test-Driven Development is a development practice where you write a failing test before writing the production code. The cycle is Red, write a small test that fails because the behavior does not exist yet; Green, write the minimum code to make that test pass; Refactor, clean up the design while keeping the test green. You repeat this in tight loops. It helps because it catches bugs at the moment of writing, drives simpler and more testable design since code is written to satisfy a test, and leaves a suite of tests that documents exactly what the code is supposed to do.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When building the National Bank of India interest calculator, instead of writing the calculator and hoping it works, you first write a tiny check that says "for one hundred thousand rupees at four percent for one year, the interest must be four thousand." It fails because there is no calculator yet, that is Red. Then you write just enough calculator code to make that check pass, that is Green. Then you tidy the code without breaking the check, that is Refactor. You keep adding one small check at a time. The result is that every rule is proven as you build it, the design stays simple because you only write what a check demands, and the checks themselves become a living description of how interest is meant to work.

**One line to remember:** TDD means write a failing test first, write just enough code to pass it, then refactor, repeating this Red-Green-Refactor loop, which catches bugs early, drives simpler testable design, and leaves tests that document the intended behavior.

sections.s2_technical:
The cycle is deliberately small and fast. In the Red step you write one focused test for a single piece of behavior that does not exist yet, and you run it to confirm it fails for the right reason, which proves the test actually exercises something and is not accidentally passing. Writing the test first forces you to decide the desired behavior and the interface before the implementation, which is a design activity disguised as testing. In the Green step you write the simplest code that makes the test pass, resisting the urge to add anything the test does not require, because unneeded code is untested code and speculative complexity. Running the test confirms Green. In the Refactor step, with a passing test as a safety net, you improve the internal structure, remove duplication, rename for clarity, extract methods, without changing behavior, rerunning the test to ensure it stays green. Then you pick the next small behavior and loop.

TDD helps in three concrete ways. It catches bugs early because a defect is detected the instant you write the code, when the context is fresh and the fix is cheap, rather than later in integration or production where diagnosis is expensive. It drives better design because writing the test first makes you design from the caller's perspective, which tends to produce small, focused units with clear interfaces and few hidden dependencies, since hard-to-test code is a signal of poor design that TDD surfaces immediately; it also naturally pushes toward dependency injection and separation of concerns because those make code testable. And it acts as documentation because the tests are executable specifications: a reader can look at the tests to understand exactly what the code does and what edge cases it handles, and unlike prose documentation these specifications cannot drift out of date because they fail if the behavior changes.

The senior nuances are that TDD is a design discipline as much as a testing one, that the tests should be small and test behavior not implementation so refactoring does not break them, that you should see the test fail before making it pass to avoid false confidence, and that TDD is most valuable for logic-rich code such as calculations, rules, and state machines, while it is applied with judgement for thin glue code or exploratory spikes. A common misunderstanding is that TDD slows you down; in logic-heavy domains it usually speeds overall delivery by preventing defects and rework and by keeping the design clean enough to change safely. In a bank, where a miscalculated interest or fee has real financial and regulatory consequences, writing the test first for every rule gives both correctness and a precise, trustworthy record of what each rule does.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must compute simple interest correctly for every scenario, and a bug means real money is wrong, so each rule should be proven as it is built. This is exactly writing the test first.

Problem 2 — The calculator must stay simple and only do what the rules require, which TDD enforces by writing only enough code to pass. This is exactly the Green discipline.

Problem 3 — The code must be cleaned safely and the tests must document the rules, which Refactor and the executable specifications provide.

In the mini-project we build an interest calculator the TDD way, showing a failing test, the minimal implementation, and a refactor, with the tests reading as a specification. We present a Java harness that plays out Red-Green-Refactor.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: interest scenarios such as one hundred thousand rupees at four percent for one and three years, and a negative principal.

Step 1: In the Red step the demo describes the first test, that simple interest on one hundred thousand at four percent for one year must be four thousand, and notes it would fail before any calculator exists, which is the point of writing the test first.

Step 2: In the Green step the minimal calculator is used and the first test passes, printing Green, because only enough code was written to satisfy that one behavior.

Step 3: A second behavior, multi-year interest, is added as another Red-to-Green step, and the test confirms twelve thousand for three years, showing the tight incremental loop.

Step 4: An edge case driven by a test, a negative principal, is checked and the calculator correctly throws, demonstrating that tests drive the handling of edge cases rather than them being an afterthought.

Step 5: In the Refactor step the math and scaling are cleaned while the original test stays green, proving behavior was preserved, and the demo notes that the accumulated tests now document the interest rules as executable specifications that cannot drift out of date.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] === RED: write the test FIRST; it would fail with no calculator ===
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] Test: SI(100000, 4%, 1yr) expected 4000.00  (fails before code exists)
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] === GREEN: minimal code makes the test pass ===
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] GREEN SI(100000,4%,1) == 4000.00
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] === Add next behavior (another RED->GREEN): multi-year ===
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] GREEN SI(100000,4%,3) == 12000.00
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] === Edge driven by a test: negative principal rejected ===
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] GREEN negative principal throws
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] === REFACTOR: cleaned math/scale with tests still GREEN (behavior unchanged) ===
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] GREEN still SI(100000,4%,1) == 4000.00
2026-10-30 10:05:40 [INFO] Tests now DOCUMENT the interest rules as executable specifications.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Pick ONE small behavior
    │
    ▼
  RED: write failing test first ──run──→ fails for the right reason
    │
    ▼
  GREEN: write MINIMUM code ──run──→ passes (nothing extra)
    │
    ▼
  REFACTOR: clean design ──run──→ still green (behavior unchanged)
    │
    └──loop to next behavior──┐
                              ▼
  Accumulated tests = executable specification (documentation)
  Benefits: bugs caught early, simpler testable design
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — TDD Workflow ═══

  ┌──────────────┐ writes ┌──────────────┐
  │ Developer    │───────▶│ Failing test │ (Red)
  └──────┬───────┘        └──────┬───────┘
         │ minimal code (Green)  │ safety net
         ▼                       ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  refactor ┌──────────────┐
  │ Production    │◀─────────│ Test suite    │ (docs + regression)
  │ code          │  green   │ (CI gate)     │
  └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Red-Green-Refactor ═══

  ┌─ Cycle ───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ RED      : one failing test (design the interface)    │
  │ GREEN    : minimum code to pass (no speculation)      │
  │ REFACTOR : clean up, tests stay green                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Benefits: early bugs | testable design | living docs
  Best for: logic-rich code (calc/rules/state machines)

  ── State Diagram: a behavior ───────────────────────────
  [NO CODE] → RED(test fails) → GREEN(passes) → REFACTOR(clean)
       → next behavior

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. write test → run → RED
  2. implement minimal → run → GREEN
  3. refactor → run → GREEN
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Test-Driven Development is a practice where I write a failing test before the production code, following the Red-Green-Refactor cycle. Red: I write one small test for a single behavior that does not exist yet and run it to confirm it fails for the right reason, which proves the test really exercises something. Green: I write the minimum code to make it pass, resisting anything the test does not require, because unneeded code is untested code. Refactor: with the passing test as a safety net I clean up the structure, remove duplication, and rename for clarity without changing behavior, rerunning to stay green. Then I pick the next small behavior and loop.

It helps in three concrete ways. It catches bugs early, because a defect is caught the instant I write the code when the context is fresh and the fix is cheap, not later in integration or production. It drives better design, because writing the test first makes me design from the caller's perspective, which produces small focused units with clear interfaces, and hard-to-test code immediately signals a design problem, so TDD naturally pushes toward dependency injection and separation of concerns. And it acts as documentation, because the tests are executable specifications that describe exactly what the code does and which edge cases it handles, and unlike prose they cannot drift out of date because they fail if the behavior changes.

The nuances I add are that TDD is a design discipline as much as a testing one, that tests should target behavior not implementation so refactoring does not break them, that I must see the test fail before making it pass to avoid false confidence, and that it is most valuable for logic-rich code like calculations and rules while applied with judgement for thin glue. At the National Bank of India I used TDD for the interest and fee calculators, writing a failing test for each rule, then the minimal code, then refactoring, and the payoff was both correctness, since a miscalculated fee has real regulatory consequences, and a precise, trustworthy, always-current record of what every rule does. Being able to explain the cycle and tie it to early bug detection, better design, and living documentation is what shows an interviewer I understand TDD as a way to build correct, well-designed, well-documented code rather than a box-ticking ritual.
